data.translation:
Since October 1, the S&P 500 is down 1.2%. Berkshire Hathaway is up 19.1%. The market has found its safe haven amid fears of AI, and on Monday we'll find out what Berkshire has done with its portfolio.

The data (CNBC, Nov. 14):
• The Class A shares have closed at all-time highs 11 times since October 1, the last four this week.
• This week: +3.9%, versus +2.5% for the S&P 500.
• Year to date, the Class B shares are up around 18% and outperforming the index by 7.5 percentage points.

My take: a 20.3-point lead over the S&P 500 in six weeks, for a company this size, is a very clear rotation. Money is paying for stability.

The 13F arrives on Monday, November 16: a snapshot of its stock holdings as of September 30. The clues are in the third-quarter 10-Q:
• $2.2 billion in pretax gains from stock sales.
• A $372 million reduction in the cost basis of its banking, insurance and financial services portfolio.
• Barron's estimates that it sold between 30 and 40 million shares of Bank of America. That would make it the ninth consecutive quarter of selling.

My calculation for Bank of America: since June 2024, Berkshire has sold 53.2% of its shares while the stock price rose 28.3%. The position is worth about $24.7 billion today. Without the sales, it would be worth about $52.7 billion. Selling a bank whose stock is rising is no oversight: it's a decision to reduce exposure to banks.

What to watch for in the 13F:
• Whether the Bank of America sale is confirmed and how large it is.
• Whether there are any new purchases or additions to existing positions during the quarter.
• A risk to the safe-haven thesis: if fears of AI ease, the money that has flowed into Berkshire could return to tech stocks and reverse some of the gains.

Educational content, not a recommendation.

Would you buy Berkshire at all-time highs as a safe haven, or do you think that safe-haven status is already priced in? 👇

result.text:
Anthropic's IPO lands Thursday with more than 900 billion dollars in spending commitments riding on it. The biggest tech IPO in years now carries the weight of much of the AI industry.

Anthropic is expected to price its shares on Wednesday and begin trading on Nasdaq under the ticker ANT on Thursday, at an expected 70 to 78 dollars a share. CNBC reports the stakes reach almost every major tech company. AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia and TSMC are collectively investing 26 billion dollars at the IPO price.

The bigger exposure is what Anthropic has promised to spend. According to its prospectus, the Claude maker has outstanding spending commitments of more than 900 billion dollars. Those are commitments, not money spent or cash in hand. They include at least 110 billion dollars with Amazon over a decade, and, per filings and partner disclosures cited by CNBC, another 400 billion dollars with other cloud providers and 300 billion dollars with data center and chip partners.

The losses are just as large. Anthropic recorded a net loss of 104 billion dollars in the first nine months of 2026, CNBC reports. The IPO could yield more than 90 billion dollars on top of 132 billion dollars in existing cash and short-term investments. "In the past, we have significantly underestimated our compute requirements," the company says in its prospectus.

Partners are already carrying some of the risk. Google, set to own about 13 percent of Anthropic after the IPO, is backstopping 19 billion dollars in lease commitments to data center firm TeraWulf, according to TeraWulf. Bank of America, Blackstone, Citigroup and Morgan Stanley have offered 63 billion dollars to buy racks of Broadcom AI chips that Anthropic will rent, with Broadcom backstopping up to 43 billion dollars.

The timing is rough. The Nasdaq fell 5.3 percent in October. Nvidia shares dropped 13 percent last week after Jensen Huang's ouster, and interim CEO Colette Kress reports quarterly results on Tuesday, two days before Anthropic debuts.

"The numbers are just staggering," Eclipse partner Joe Fath told CNBC. For American investors and the companies building America's AI capacity, Thursday is a referendum on whether those numbers can be financed.
